NHL Player Props: How Shots on Goal, Points, and Goalie Lines Get Priced

Published October 17, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Hockey came to player props later than football and basketball did, and it still shows in how the markets behave. A shots-on-goal line and a goaltender saves line look similar on a bet slip — both are just a number with an over and an under — but they're built from almost nothing in common. One tracks a skater's role and shot volume. The other tracks how much rubber an entire opposing team is going to throw at a net. Treating them the same way is probably the single most common mistake in NHL prop betting.

Why NHL props are priced differently than other sports

An NFL passing-yards prop or an NBA points prop benefits from decades of granular tracking and a betting public that's been pricing those markets aggressively for years. NHL props are a newer, thinner market by comparison — fewer books post a full props board for every game, limits are generally lower, and the public betting volume behind any single line is smaller. That combination matters for a bettor: thinner markets move less efficiently, which can occasionally create value, but it also means a line can sit a touch off true probability simply because fewer sharp dollars have pushed against it yet.

It also means the underlying stat categories vary more in how predictable they are. Shots on goal happen dozens of times a game and are driven heavily by playing time and role. Goals and points are comparatively rare events shaped by randomness as much as skill. Treating all three prop types with one mental model is where a lot of recreational bettors go wrong.

Shots on goal: the volume market

Shots on goal (SOG) is the highest-volume, most heavily bet skater prop in hockey, and for good reason: a top-line forward getting 18-20 minutes a night will typically attempt somewhere in the range of three to five shots on goal in a given game, which gives the market a reasonably stable baseline to price from. Lines for a team's primary shooters usually sit in the 2.5-to-4.5 range, with secondary scorers and depth players priced well below that.

What makes SOG attractive to bettors isn't just the volume — it's that a player can hit the over without needing anything to actually go in the net. A player can fire five shots, get stopped five times, and still cash an over 3.5 ticket. That decouples the prop from goal-scoring luck to a meaningful degree, which is part of why SOG tends to be treated as the more "skill-driven" and less variance-heavy of the common skater props.

The shot volume itself is driven by role (power-play time, even-strength deployment, whether a player is a shoot-first winger or a pass-first center), game state (teams trailing tend to shoot more as the game goes on), and opponent shot-suppression — a matchup against a team that blocks a lot of shots or controls the neutral zone well will tend to push SOG totals down league-wide, not just for one player.

Points, goals, and assists: the scarcity markets

Points props (goals plus assists) and anytime-goalscorer markets sit on the opposite end of the predictability spectrum from SOG. Even an elite goal-scorer converts only a fraction of their shot attempts, and a strong playmaker can go multiple games without registering a point despite generating plenty of good looks. That scarcity is exactly why these props carry higher payout odds than SOG overs — the book is pricing a genuinely less frequent outcome, not just offering a better number.

Assists carry an extra wrinkle: they're partly a function of teammates finishing plays a player sets up, which means a playmaker can have a quiet "stat line" game while still generating the same quality of underlying offense they always do. This is why points props are often priced using a blend of individual shot/chance generation and the finishing ability of the players around them, rather than the bettor's own stats alone.

Why this matters: a shots-on-goal over and a points over on the same player are not twin bets with similar risk — one is closer to a volume-based coin that's slightly weighted in your favor, the other is closer to betting that a relatively rare event lands on a specific night.

Goalie props: priced off the other team, not the goalie

This is the part that trips up bettors coming from other sports. A quarterback's passing-yards line is priced mostly around that quarterback and his own offense. A goalie's saves line is priced mostly around the opposing team — because a save only happens when the other team puts a shot on net. An elite goaltender behind a defense that allows very few shots can have a lower saves total than a mediocre goaltender stuck behind a leaky, high-event team, simply because the mediocre goaltender is going to see far more rubber.

That's why goalie saves props move heavily on pace and shot-volume projections for the matchup as a whole, not on the goaltender's save percentage alone. A goalie's save percentage still matters for goals-against and win-probability markets, but for the saves total specifically, the opponent's shot-generation tendency is usually the bigger input.

Shots on goal (top-line skater)2.5 – 4.5Ice time, role, shot-first tendency

What actually moves these lines before puck drop

A handful of factors show up across almost every NHL prop market, though they pull in different directions depending on the bet:

  • Starting goaltender confirmation. As with moneylines, NHL starters are often confirmed late, and goalie props in particular shouldn't be bet far ahead of a confirmed starter — a late scratch changes the entire bet.
  • Power-play unit placement. A player on the top power-play unit sees a disproportionate share of a team's most dangerous offensive looks, which lifts both shot and point props well beyond what their 5-on-5 role alone would suggest.
  • Back-to-back scheduling. Fatigue from a dense schedule can quietly suppress shot volume and ice time for skaters, and can factor into which goaltender even starts.
  • Pace of the matchup. A projected high-event, up-tempo game lifts shot and save totals across the board; a projected low-event, defensive game suppresses them — this is a team-level signal that affects every individual prop in the game.
  • Line combinations and injuries. A forward moved up to a better line, or a teammate's injury opening up power-play time, can shift a player's prop profile overnight, often before the market has fully adjusted.

Common mistakes bettors make with NHL props

  • Betting a goalie saves total like a goalie-skill bet. It's closer to a bet on the opposing team's shot volume than a bet on the goaltender's talent.
  • Assuming a strong recent stretch of points will continue. Scoring in hockey is streaky by nature; a hot week often says more about puck luck and finishing variance than a durable change in role or usage.
  • Ignoring power-play unit changes. A demotion off the top power-play unit can quietly gut a points prop's value even when a player's 5-on-5 role is unchanged.
  • Treating SOG and points props as equally predictable. They aren't — SOG is a volume stat with a tighter range of outcomes, while points carry more game-to-game variance.

Frequently asked questions

Why do goalie saves props move so much based on the opposing team?

Because a save can only happen in response to a shot the other team actually takes. A goaltender facing a high-volume, fast-paced offense will tend to have a higher saves total than an equally skilled goaltender facing a low-volume, defensive-minded team, independent of either goaltender's individual ability.

Is shots on goal a more predictable prop than points?

Generally, yes. Shots on goal happen far more often per game than goals or points, giving the market a larger, steadier sample to price from, while points and goals are comparatively rare events more exposed to night-to-night variance.

How much does power-play time matter for NHL props?

A lot. Power-play minutes generate a disproportionate share of a team's most dangerous scoring chances, so a player's spot on the top power-play unit can meaningfully lift their shots and points props beyond what their even-strength role alone would suggest.

Should I wait for the starting goaltender before betting goalie props?

It's generally the safer approach. NHL starters are often not confirmed until close to puck drop, and a goalie prop bet placed well before that confirmation carries real risk of being based on the wrong goaltender entirely.
